
### spanning tree  {.smaller}


* given a general network, only activate subset of links
* … such that network is tree 

   * that is only one path between each node
 
<hr class="vspace" />
* allows us to do flooding strategy
* makes simple MAC learning/broadcast just work


### centralized spanning tree?  {.smaller}


* one algorithm you might learn in DSA2: 
<hr class="vspace" />
* mark one node called <i>the root</i> as ‘in the tree’
* repeatedly:  

   * add the ‘[first]{.fragment fragment-index=2 .custom .myem-only}’ link that goes to a node not in the tree
   * mark newly connected node as ‘in the tree’
 
<hr class="vspace" />
* result = spanning tree


### a careful ordering  {.smaller}


* algorithm works with any idea of which link/node is first 
<hr class="vspace" />
* we'll choose a particular ordering (for reasons you'll see later) 
<hr class="vspace" />
* root (first node) is one with earliest ‘name’
* links closer to the root before further links
* links from nodes with earlier names before later ones


### spanning tree example 



::: {.r-stack .my-full}
![](/routing-intro/texfig/spanning-tree-example.figure-1.svg){.fragment .fade-out fragment-index=2 fig-alt="Graph with bidirectional connections: A to B, G; G to F, E; B to D, E; F t E, G; E to F, G, D."}

![](/routing-intro/texfig/spanning-tree-example.figure-2.svg){.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=2 fig-alt="The connection from A to B has higher priority than that from A to G."}

![](/routing-intro/texfig/spanning-tree-example.figure-3.svg){.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=3 fig-alt="The spanning tree is started with root A and child B."}

![](/routing-intro/texfig/spanning-tree-example.figure-4.svg){.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=4 fig-alt="Then the connection from A to G is added, so the spanning tree is: G-A, A-B"}

![](/routing-intro/texfig/spanning-tree-example.figure-5.svg){.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=5 fig-alt="Then we examine the possible links to add. G-B is rejected because it introduces no new nodes. B-D is first priority because of the node lettering. G-F is second priority."}


:::


### detecting ‘mistakes’  {.smaller}


* this method: consistent results every time 
<hr class="vspace" />
* but assumes we start from scratch
* we're going to want a way of doing this dynamically 
<hr class="vspace" />
* let's say we find a wrong configuration ---
* can we fix it?


### fixing wrong links 



::: {.r-stack .my-full}
![](/routing-intro/texfig/spanning-tree-fixing-wrong-links.figure-1.svg){.fragment .fade-out fragment-index=2 fig-alt="Initially the spanning tree selected is A-B, B-G, G-F, F-E, B-D."}

![](/routing-intro/texfig/spanning-tree-fixing-wrong-links.figure-2.svg){.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=2 fig-alt="We consider replacing B-G with A-G."}

![](/routing-intro/texfig/spanning-tree-fixing-wrong-links.figure-3.svg){.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=3 fig-alt="We consider having E connected via F versus via D."}

![](/routing-intro/texfig/spanning-tree-fixing-wrong-links.figure-4.svg){.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=4 fig-alt="Now the spanning tree is: F-G, G-A, A-B, B-D, D-E."}

![](/routing-intro/texfig/spanning-tree-fixing-wrong-links.figure-5.svg){.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=5 fig-alt="We consider replacing D-E with G-E."}


:::

::: {.myoverbox .fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=2 .low }

A-G should replace B-G because it moves G closer to the root A.

:::

::: {.myoverbox .fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=3}

*  D-E and F-E:<br/>
   *  same distance from root, but...
   *  D before F, so D-E wins

:::

::: {.myoverbox .fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=5}

*  G--E and D--E:
   *  G--E closer to root, so wins
   *  (even though D before G)

:::




### spanning tree protocol  {.smaller}


* each node tracks: 

   * what it believes is root of tree
   * its link toward root of tree
   * its distance to root of tree
   * which other nodes think it's closer to root of tree

* periodically sends information to neighbors
* when receiving information, update: 

   * root to lower ID number (if possible)
   * link to lower-distance link  (if possible)
   * link to lower-ID, same-distance link (if possible)
   * which other nodes think it is closer



### some example updates 



::: {.r-stack .my-full}
![](/routing-intro/texfig/spanning-tree-some-example-updates.figure-1.svg){.fragment .fade-out fragment-index=2 fig-alt="Same network as before: A-B, A-G, B-G, G-F, G-E, F-E, B-D, D-E"}

![](/routing-intro/texfig/spanning-tree-some-example-updates.figure-2.svg){.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=2 fig-alt="Each node tracks three variables: the tree root, the distance to the root, and the link up toward the root. Initially all nodes have a root of themselves, a distance of 0, and no link to the root."}

![](/routing-intro/texfig/spanning-tree-some-example-updates.figure-3.svg){.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=3 fig-alt="Node E sends an update to its neighbors D, F and G."}

![](/routing-intro/texfig/spanning-tree-some-example-updates.figure-4.svg){.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=4 fig-alt="As a result of node E's message F and G update their status: F has root=E, distance 1, link F-E; G has root=E, distance 1, link G-E. Node D does not update since D comes before E, so its old status of D being the root is better than node E's proposal."}

![](/routing-intro/texfig/spanning-tree-some-example-updates.figure-5.svg){.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=5 fig-alt="Node D sends an update to its neighbors E and B."}

![](/routing-intro/texfig/spanning-tree-some-example-updates.figure-6.svg){.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=6 fig-alt="As a result of node D's updates, node E changes its status to root=D, distance 1, link E-D. Since node E has not updated its neighbors F and G again yet, they still have node E as a root (even though this temporarily disagrees with node E's information). B does not update its state as a result of node D's update since B comes before D, so D's proposal of D being a root is inferior to B's current state."}


:::


### spanning trees in practice (1)  {.smaller}


* commonly used on Ethernet for switches
* links not in spanning tree are ‘blocked’ 

   * not used for normal traffic
   * assumption: would cause loop $\rightarrow$ infinite packets

* delay before activating port 

   * avoid temporary routing loops while figuring out tree

* periodically send updates to all neighbors 

   * order of seconds



### spanning tree in practice (2) 


* real protocol supports variable ‘cost’ for links 

   * so ‘distance to root’ might be lower for faster links

* modern variant (Rapid Spanning Tree Protocol) selects ‘‘backup’’ port to root  

   * goal: faster switchover on failure
